title: GDPR & Data Protection
blurb: How to look after guest, wedding and staff information, and what to do if something goes wrong.
siteNotes: Who covers if the General Manager is away when a breach happens
Where booking sheets and function orders are locked away
Venue rules on screen locking, passwords and personal phones
How a guest asks to see their information, and how it reaches the General Manager
legalNotes: Data protection law: UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2018/12
CHECK: the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 amended parts of UK GDPR (including how requests for information are handled); the trainer does not mention it. Confirm nothing here is out of date.

CHECK: the trainer says to report a breach to the General Manager. Confirm the venue procedure also covers telling the Information Commissioner's Office where required; no time limit is stated in the session.
CHECK: the trainer says a breach can lead to a large fine. Kept as a general statement with no figure.
Need to know, locking screens, strong passwords and double-checking email addresses are standard good practice under the security principle of UK GDPR.

cards.title: GDPR & Data Protection
cards.body:
By the end of this session you can:
- say what "need to know" means for your job
- keep guest and staff information secure
- report a breach or a request quickly

cards.title: We handle personal information daily
cards.body: We handle guest names, phone numbers, card details, booking notes, wedding plans and staff records. Data protection law (GDPR) makes sure we look after it responsibly. A breach can cause real harm to real people and can lead to a large fine.

cards.title: Only look at what you need
cards.body: Only access personal information you actually need to do your job. Never out of curiosity, and never to look up a friend, a celebrity guest or an ex.

left.title: Do
items: Look up what your job needs

right.title: Do not
items: Look up a celebrity guest for fun
Post guest details on social media

cards.title: Practical ways to keep it safe
The wrong address is a breach
cards.body:
Sending guest details to the wrong person is one of the most common breaches there is. Always double-check the address before you send.

> A moment's check protects the guest and the business.

cards.title: Report it straight away
cards.body: A lost booking book, a laptop left on a train or an email to the wrong guest is a possible breach. Report it to the General Manager straight away so we can limit the damage.

items.title: Spot it
items.text: A lost sheet, a wrong email.

cards.title: If a guest asks what we hold
cards.body: A guest can ask to see the information we hold about them. Do not guess what to say. Pass the request to the General Manager to handle properly.

items.title: Pass it to the General Manager
items.text: Do not guess or promise anything.

items.title: Note who asked
items.text: So it can be followed up.

cards.title: Remember
cards.body:
- Need to know: only information your job needs
- Lock away paperwork and lock your screen
- Strong, private passwords, and check email addresses
- Any loss or mistake goes to the General Manager straight away
- Guest requests to see their information go to the General Manager

cards.q: What is the "need to know" principle?
options: Tell the team everything you know about a guest
Keep guest information to yourself, even from managers
Only access information your job needs
Look up guests whenever you are curious
cards.why: Only access personal information you actually need to do your job, never out of curiosity.

cards.q: It's fine to look up a celebrity guest's details out of curiosity.
cards.why: Never look up a friend, a celebrity guest or an ex. You only access what your job needs.

options: Nothing to worry about
A possible data breach to report
Only a problem if a guest complains
A guest's problem, not ours
cards.why: Lost paperwork is a possible breach. Report it straight away so the damage can be limited.

cards.q: Sending guest details to the wrong email address is a common data breach.
cards.why: It is one of the most common breaches there is. Always double-check the address first.

cards.q: When you step away from a screen you should…
options: Lock it
Leave it open, as you will be back
Turn the brightness down
Close the window, but stay logged in
cards.why: Locking your screen stops anyone else seeing or using guest information.

cards.q: Guest information is fine to share on social media.
cards.why: Guest and colleague information is confidential. It is not for gossip or social media.

cards.q: Who should you report a data breach to?
options: The guest it affects
Whoever is on reception
Nobody, if you fixed it yourself
The General Manager
cards.why: Report to the General Manager straight away so the damage can be limited.

options: Strong and private
Shared with the team
Written on the till
The same as everyone's
cards.why: Use strong passwords and keep them to yourself.

cards.q: A guest can ask to see the personal information we hold about them.
cards.why: If they ask, pass the request to the General Manager to handle properly.

cards.q: Name one practical way to keep paper records secure.
options: Leave them under the till
Keep them in your coat pocket
Lock them away in a drawer
Pin them up in the staff room
cards.why: Paperwork like booking sheets and function orders should be locked away.
